overview.metric.readiness.title: Project readiness
overview.metric.readiness.lead: A quick glance: whether the project has enough foundation to move forward with confidence.
paragraphs: The percentage blends five directions: project base, team work, links between sections, evidence freshness, and strategy logic.
A low score is not a verdict—it signals which hall block to raise next.
related: Overview → why readiness looks like this
tips: Open the block with gaps below—that shows where to start.
Add data in any order; the score updates after you save.

overview.metric.jtbd.title: Customer jobs
overview.metric.jtbd.lead: How many customer jobs are recorded in the project.
paragraphs: This is the foundation of the offer: without customer jobs it is hard to say honestly who the product is for and why it matters.
Only jobs tied to the selected project are counted here.
tips: Capture 3–5 pivotal jobs manually or from interviews.
Set priority—it helps choose focus.

overview.metric.value_props.title: Value propositions
overview.metric.value_props.lead: How many drafts and versions of the promise to the customer.
paragraphs: Each offer rests on customer jobs and is backed by evidence.
Statuses—draft, review, approved—show how mature the wording is.
tips: Pick a customer job first, then create the offer.
Back the promise with facts from project evidence.

overview.metric.evidence.title: Evidence
overview.metric.evidence.lead: How many evidence units are tied to the project as strategic foundation.
paragraphs: Not just files: evidence confirms promises, conclusions, and team decisions.
Materials linked to the selected project appear here.
tips: Upload transcripts, reports, and decks—then reference them in offers and research.
The “Open content” button leads to full evidence management.

overview.readiness_cycle.title: Project readiness cycle
overview.readiness_cycle.lead: A map of what is already aligned in strategy and what is still missing.
paragraphs: The hall follows a simple chain: customer job → offer → audience → promotion → team work.
The “Gaps” block shows where the chain is still weak.
related: All sections on the campaign map
tips: Use the gap list as a guide for your next move.
You do not have to close everything at once—keep focus on the nearest release or campaign.

overview.latest_swot.title: Latest market picture
overview.latest_swot.lead: A quick slice of strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats for the project.
paragraphs: Shows strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats from the latest completed or current analysis.
If there is no analysis yet—go to “Market and competitors” and create one manually or with an Oracle.
tips: Refresh the market picture when the market shifts or after major research.
The short summary on the tile is handy for team syncs.

overview.recent_jtbd.title: Latest customer jobs
overview.recent_jtbd.lead: Recently added or current customer jobs.
paragraphs: Shows momentum: what you captured lately in research or by hand.
The full list and editing live in the Customer jobs section.
tips: If the list is empty—start with one sharp pain job.
Review priorities before drafting an offer.

overview.value_props.title: Value propositions on overview
overview.value_props.lead: A slice of current promise wording.
paragraphs: See headline, status, and the core promise without leaving the section.
Linked customer jobs show why this promise matters.
tips: Keep several versions for different audiences.
Carry approved wording into content and landing pages.

overview.evidence_research.title: Evidence and research
overview.evidence_research.lead: Briefs and files that back the strategy.
paragraphs: At the top—research briefs: what you need to learn or what you already found out.
Below—fragments of project evidence: excerpts and descriptions of attached materials.
tips: Create a research question before a deep dive—so the task is not lost.
Tie research outcomes to project evidence.

setup.companies.title: Houses
setup.companies.lead: Top level: brand, market, and shared context.
paragraphs: Every project and the whole marketing march live inside the selected house.
Search helps when you manage a large portfolio of brands or directions.
tips: Fill in industry and website—Oracles and summaries use this in their work.
Edit and delete via icons in the list row.

setup.company_form.title: Create / edit house
setup.company_form.lead: Minimum profile to enter the hall.
paragraphs: Name is required; the rest strengthens recommendations and Oracle briefings.
Website is validated for a correct URL—include a protocol or domain.
tips: In the description, briefly: who the customer is and how you earn.
Edit mode opens from the pencil in the list.

setup.projects.title: Projects
setup.projects.lead: Working unit: campaign, study, or initiative inside a house.
paragraphs: Customer jobs, offer, market, competitors, research, and Oracle questions are tied to the selected project.
Archiving does not delete data—you can restore activity later.
tips: Before analysis, confirm the header shows the right project.
Use priority to steer the team’s attention.

setup.project_form.title: Create / edit project
setup.project_form.lead: Sets name, description, category, priority, and which hall sections apply.
paragraphs: Enabled sections determine which hall blocks matter—often set by the default template.
Editing lets you change name and parameters without changing the project identifier.
tips: In the description, state goal and audience—it helps Oracles and summaries.
After creation, switch to Overview to see the empty project.

setup.team.title: Project team
setup.team.lead: Members and lead; invites only among mutual friends.
paragraphs: The lead adds and removes members; removing someone revokes evidence shares issued to them.
Lead transfer is only to an active member—a separate action after they join the team.
tips: Without a selected project this block stays empty.
Members who are not the lead see the roster but not invite forms.

jtbd.list.title: Customer jobs (list)
jtbd.list.lead: The unified list of customer jobs for the current project.
paragraphs: From here you edit, delete, and mark jobs for use in the offer.
Search from two characters; CSV export for collaborative work.
tips: Choose 1–5 jobs for a focused offer.
Tags help filter in summaries and with the Oracle.

jtbd.manual_create.title: Create a customer job manually
jtbd.manual_create.lead: Structured form: situation, motivation, and expected outcome.
paragraphs: Situation, motivation, and expected outcome are required for clarity.
Category and priority help segment offers later.
tips: Write from the customer’s view: “when I … I want … so that …”.
Importance 0–10—for prioritization within the team.

jtbd.ai_extract.title: Extraction from interviews
jtbd.ai_extract.lead: Bulk creation of customer jobs from unstructured text.
paragraphs: Paste a transcript or notes (from 100 characters); set the maximum number of jobs.
The Oracle will suggest wording—you can edit it later in the list.
tips: The richer the interview, the sharper the result.
Have a human review wording before you lock the offer.

value.list.title: Current value propositions
value.list.lead: All promise versions for the project.
paragraphs: Change status right in the list; delete via the trash icon.
Each tile shows evidence and linked customer jobs.
tips: Keep a draft for experiments and a separate one for execution.
Copy and CSV—for alignment with the team.

value.create.title: Create value proposition
value.create.lead: Assembles the promise from selected customer jobs.
paragraphs: Headlines can stay empty—the hall may generate them from jobs.
Evidence is an ordered list of supporting points.
tips: Mark customer jobs first in the adjacent block on the right.
A one-line value statement makes client review easier.

value.select_jtbd.title: Customer job selection for the offer
value.select_jtbd.lead: Explicit link: which customer jobs this offer serves.
paragraphs: Selected jobs are saved together with the offer.
Several jobs—for a broad product; one job—for tight positioning.
tips: Do not mix incompatible audiences in one offer without a clear “for whom”.
Revisit the selection after new interviews.

analysis.swot_list.title: Market analysis
analysis.swot_list.lead: History of strategic snapshots and creating a new analysis.
paragraphs: Extra description is optional but helps capture market nuance.
The list uses virtualization when you have many versions.
tips: Refresh after fresh customer jobs or research.
Export to CSV for presentations.

analysis.swot_manual.title: Manual SWOT
analysis.swot_manual.lead: Enter factors line by line after a joint review.
paragraphs: Each quadrant is its own field; one line = one factor.
Best when the team already structured material on a board.
tips: Do not duplicate what you already have—create a new entry with refinements.
Keep the executive summary brief for leadership.

analysis.competitors.title: Competitors
analysis.competitors.lead: Cards for players shaping your market position.
paragraphs: Used in strategy, the offer, and evidence discussions.
Search and export work like other hall lists.
tips: Record pricing line and competitor promise—it shapes differentiation.
Update when rivals ship new products.

analysis.competitor_form.title: Add competitor
paragraphs: Minimum—name and positioning; strengths, weaknesses, and pricing deepen the value.
Data joins the shared list and helps Oracles answer more precisely.
tips: Use objective wording—avoid labels without facts.
Tie to a specific project so markets do not mix.

evidence.research_list.title: Research briefs
evidence.research_list.lead: Registry of “what we need to learn” for the project.
paragraphs: Each brief may reference evidence with the outcome.
Statuses reflect the lifecycle from draft to archive.
tips: A clear research request saves analyst time.
List goals explicitly—they are easy to track.

evidence.research_create.title: Create research
evidence.research_create.lead: Accept a new brief into the work queue.
paragraphs: Research type sets the frame: market, customer, competitors, or customer jobs.
Result summary can be filled now if conclusions are already known.
tips: Do not leave the request empty—it is the key field for whoever executes.
Align priority with the product owner.

evidence.unified_content.title: Project evidence
evidence.unified_content.lead: Files and materials for the project in the hall’s unified store.
paragraphs: Here you see name, type, update time, and a fragment of extracted text.
Full management—through the evidence section (“Open content” button).
tips: Refresh the list after uploading new files.
Use descriptions so Oracles find relevant quotes.

evidence.cycle_explainer.title: Evidence cycle
evidence.cycle_explainer.lead: How this section fits into the hall.
paragraphs: Research sets questions; project evidence holds answers and facts.
Oracles use both layers so answers stay grounded in files.
tips: Keep at least one brief in active status for the current focus.
Sync research outcomes with PDF and document uploads.

chat.context.title: Question context
chat.context.lead: What the Oracle actually sees when answering.
paragraphs: The selected house and project from the hall header are applied.
Example questions suggest wording for strategic decisions.
tips: Change project in the header if answers feel like the wrong product.
Copy important answers into the offer or research by hand.

chat.dialog.title: Dialog with the Oracle
chat.dialog.lead: Strategic questions and answers on hall data.
paragraphs: Messages do not replace saving artifacts—use campaign map sections to lock decisions.
Ctrl/Cmd+Enter sends from the keyboard.
tips: Start by clarifying audience or hypothesis.
“New conversation” clears history on screen.
